The consumer of this output has no mechanism for distinguishing what was found from what was generated. This paper formalizes the problem as narrative completion under uncertainty and advances a falsifiable hypothesis: that the fused stream is nonetheless separable, because the boundary between evidential grounding and generative interpolation is geometrically decidable from transformer hidden states and the intensity of interpolation is quantifiable along a continuous gradient. The proposed instrument is a synesthetic provenance decomposition in which an auxiliary classification head, running parallel to the primary language modeling head, projects the shared hidden-state representations onto a continuous provenance gradient at every token position. Drawing on the linear representation hypothesis and the approximate orthogonality of semantic subspaces in highdimensional transformer embeddings, the paper proposes that provenance attributes are recoverable from the residual stream without distorting the geometry on which the primary unembedding head depends. The architecture produces a three-channel continuous signal analogous to RGB color depth, decomposing each token's generation into retrieval-grounded (R), parametric-memory (G), and generative-interpolative (B) components. The paper connects this decomposition to directed persistent path-homology and the complement set formalism for measuring structured absence, argues that the boundary between measurement and generation in LLM output is a continuous gradient rather than a discrete threshold, presents falsification protocols including dimensionality reduction stress tests against Cover's theorem, and specifies a concrete experimental proto…

The consumer of this output has no mechanism for distinguishing what was found from what was generated. This paper formalizes the problem as narrative completion under uncertainty and advances a falsifiable hypothesis: that the fused stream is nonetheless separable, because the boundary between evidential grounding and generative interpolation is geometrically decidable from transformer hidden states and the intensity of interpolation is quantifiable along a continuous gradient. The proposed instrument is a synesthetic provenance decomposition in which an auxiliary classification head, running parallel to the primary language modeling head, projects the shared hidden-state representations onto a continuous provenance gradient at every token position. Drawing on the linear representation hypothesis and the approximate orthogonality of semantic subspaces in highdimensional transformer embeddings, the paper proposes that provenance attributes are recoverable from the residual stream without distorting the geometry on which the primary unembedding head depends. The architecture produces a three-channel continuous signal analogous to RGB color depth, decomposing each token's generation into retrieval-grounded (R), parametric-memory (G), and generative-interpolative (B) components.
